text:
THE HARDEST TAPE IN YEARS. 

This is not the worst market, but arguably the hardest one to win in. $NBIS can rally double digits one day and give it all back over the next two. $SPY and $QQQ reclaim key levels only to lose them again. Earnings beats are getting sold, misses are getting rewarded, and even strong guidance is no guarantee of a rally. Meanwhile, sticky inflation, rising yields, uncertainty around the Fed, and the leadership shock at $NVDA have added another layer of unpredictability. The AI story hasn’t disappeared, but the market has moved from asking who benefits from AI to who ultimately pays for it. Capex, debt, funding and cash flow now matter as much as demand. In this environment, being right about the company, the earnings, or even the macro isn’t enough if the market disagrees with your timing. You can get four out of five things right and still lose money. That’s why this is a market for discipline, patience and proper position sizing, not oversized conviction. Know what you own, know why you own it, keep cash available, and don’t let short-term volatility force long-term decisions. Easy markets make everyone look like a genius. Difficult markets reveal who actually has a process. The edge right now isn’t predicting every move. It’s surviving the uncertainty long enough for your thesis to play out.

Starship’s plasma blackout explained, and why SpaceX lands it with engines instead of parachutes for Mars:

Kate Tice: “Reentry is typically a portion of flight where we don’t have communications with the spacecraft, because it’s reentering at or around orbital velocity. That’s roughly eight kilometers per second, or about five miles per second. And at those speeds, the spacecraft is moving through the atmosphere so quickly that a plasma field around the vehicle starts to develop.”

Jessie Anderson: “And that blanket of plasma distorts communication frequencies, so it’s not uncommon to experience brief blackouts in communication.”

Jessie Anderson: “Starship is designed to land on Mars, where there are no runways or other humans to help out. So we’re doing propulsive landing instead of more traditional means like parachutes. That’s because propulsive landing enables more rapid reusability.”

Some personal thoughts on $NVDA and Jensen.

The cut feels rushed to me.

On Sunday, the board said it had confidence in him. By Thursday, he was gone, effective immediately. This is a founder who built the company over 30+ years and put it at the center of the entire AI build-out, and the exit came with no permanent successor, an investigation still open, and earnings days away.

I'm not defending the personal stuff. That's on him, and he owned it. But there's a difference between accountability and a decision made under a week of headline pressure. Boards usually move slower on something this big, especially when the facts are still coming in.

When things move this fast, I tend to think we haven't heard the full story yet, one way or another.

As a trader, my job isn't to pick a side in the drama. It's to watch how price handles it. But as someone who's watched what he built, it feels like a strange way for that chapter to end.

We'll see what 11/17 brings.

There are two schools of thought on how markets work.

Efficient markets: participants are rational, and all known information is already in the price.

Irrational markets: cognitive biases like overreaction, underreaction, herding, loss aversion and anchoring push prices away from fair value.

Those mispricings persist. Momentum, pre/post-earnings drift, bubbles and crashes all come from them, and limits to arbitrage keep rational traders from fully closing the gap.

That gap is where we do our work.

Most stocks do not go up in a straight line. They go up, they fall apart, and then they go up again — and the fall is where the money is made, if the story is still true.

$PLTR went to $45 in early 2021. Then it fell to $7-8, and the bottom printed near $6. More than an 80% drawdown. Everyone wrote it off. The business kept building — government contracts, then commercial, then AI — and the stock went to $207. Then it fell again, nearly 50%, to about $107. And then it went to $209.

That is the whole lesson. A 50-80% pullback is not always a broken stock. Sometimes it is the same stock, the same story, at a price that makes sense again. The market does not hand out second chances quietly — it hands them out while everyone is busy calling the name dead.

Revisit the names you liked at the top. Check if the story changed or only the price did. If the story is intact and the price is half of what it was, that is not a warning. That is the opportunity.

$SPCX - SpaceX aborted its Super Heavy booster catch attempt during Friday's 15th Starship test flight, diverting the rocket offshore, where it flipped and exploded in the ocean. The setback complicates Elon Musk's goal of making Starship fully reusable.

* Booster Failure: Launch and stage separation succeeded, but mission control canceled the catch just over five minutes into flight. SpaceX has not identified the cause.

* Starship Mission: The upper stage reached orbit and is scheduled to complete 14 orbits over 22 hours, deploy 26 V3 Starlink satellites and return to Starbase for its first catch attempt.

* Reusability: SpaceX has caught Super Heavy boosters three times but has never caught Starship's upper stage. Flight 15 was intended to recover both stages for the first time.

* Expansion Plans: Starship is central to NASA contracts, proposed orbital AI data centers and Moon and Mars missions. Musk targets more frequent launches next year, supported by a planned Louisiana launch site.

en_summary: I've seen a lot of commentary around $SE sales & marketing spend, but numbers in context: lag between S&M and revenue (Q3 2023 +$424m S&M vs +$215m rev, next q +$306m rev vs +$49m S&M); latest Q2 2026 +$690m rev vs +$246m S&M, Q3 +$795m vs +$227m ($3.50 incremental rev per $ S&M); question is return generated, latest numbers suggest meaningful growth.
text:
I've seen a lot of commentary around $SE sales & marketing spend, but I think it's worth putting the numbers into context.

A few things stand out:

1. The relationship isn't always immediate. 
In Q3 2023, incremental S&M spend increased by $424m against $215m of incremental revenue. The following quarter, incremental revenue rose to $306m while incremental S&M spend fell to just $49m. There can clearly be a lag.

2. Look at the latest numbers. 
In Q2 2026, incremental revenue was $690m against $246m of incremental S&M. In Q3, that improved to $795m against $227m. That's $3.50 of incremental revenue for every additional dollar of S&M.

3. Monetisation and GMV growth aren't mutually exclusive. 
Higher take rates are positive, but sustainability depends on maintaining competitive seller economics and consumer value.

For me, the question isn't simply how much $SE is spending on S&M, but what return it's generating. The latest numbers suggest the investment is translating into meaningful revenue growth.

text:
$MSOS, the largest cannabis ETF, is the tail that wags the dog of weed stocks.
It might be the worst thing that has ever happened to cannabis investors as...
It is a liquid ETF comprised of illiquid cannabis equities.
That is a toxic combination that rarely has a good ending - regardless of the industry that the ETF might serve.
Unfortunately, what has made matters worse has been (an arguably) poorly executed allocation strategy of the portfolio manager. (A good example of this was the misallocation of (selling) $GTBIF (our favorite stock in the sector) and using the proceeds to buy $GLAS)  Note: The guy that first understood that $MSOS could be value destructive to cannabis investors was the CEO of $GTBIF @Bkov9 - but few listened to his protestations.
Now $MSOS has a near $30 million debit balance (ergo it is on margin) because of the aforementioned portfolio strategy and recent redemptions.
This saddens me as it has hurt investors in a space that has promise because of a changing and improving regulatory landscape (leading to a more equitable tax situation among other factors), stable industry fundamentals and an improving quality of company managements.  
At some point in time the schism between upside opportunity and the current $MSOS share price will provide a unique opportunity - even despite the $MSOS headwind.
Unfortunately (again), many retail investors have been decimated before this has occurred - and have not been able to hold on to their investments in cannabis.

en_summary: I suspect Renaissance, a quant firm, didn't "know" about Jensen, they just followed their quant signals. Momentum peaked, vol spiked, so high-beta exposure got cut. Mark Stevens, a $NVDA board member, sold ~$946M of NVDA with no 10b5-1 plan, discretionary. Timing correlation ≠ insider trading, but worth pulling. (Quoted: Renaissance sold $1.42B of Nvidia weeks before Jensen quit, 13F 43 days late)
text: I suspect  Renaissance, a quant firm, didn't "know" about Jensen—they just followed their quant signals. Momentum peaked, vol spiked, so high-beta exposure got cut across the board. Timing correlation ≠ insider trading, but it's the thread worth pulling.
